Returning to 'total = 0' would reset the running total on every pass and the chart would print the last value rather than the sum; returning to the first READ box would make that box part of the loop and leave the diamond with a second entry from above that is never used. READ k appears twice because the loop's condition tests k, so k must already hold a value the first time the diamond is reached - hence the priming read before the diamond - and each pass must refresh k before the condition is tested again - hence the read at the end of the body, whose flowline is the back-arrow. The pseudocode has the same duplication, READ k once before WHILE and once as the last line of the body. If it is drawn only once inside the loop, the diamond is reached before any value has been read, so k is undefined at the first test and the chart is untraceable; and if k is assumed to start at 0 the condition k <> 0 is false immediately, the body never runs and the chart prints 0 for every input. If it is drawn only once before the loop, k keeps its first value for ever, so a non-zero first value makes the condition stay true, the back-arrow is taken on every pass, the No branch is never reached and the STOP is unreachable - an infinite loop adding the same number to the total for ever.

recapCandidates.topic: The chain rule - why the inner derivative is not optional
recapCandidates.whyMisunderstood: The chain rule is the single most-dropped mark in first-year calculus, because its output looks right without the inner derivative. A student who writes d/dx sin(3x) = cos(3x) has produced something with the correct shape - a cosine, the right argument - and nothing in the expression flags the missing factor of 3, so the error survives self-checking, unlike a botched product rule which usually looks visibly wrong. Underneath sit three deeper confusions. First, students never consciously decompose the function into outer and inner parts, so they cannot apply a rule whose statement is entirely about that split. Second, they treat the power rule as attaching to whatever is inside the brackets: d/dx (x^2 + 1)^5 becomes 5(x^2 + 1)^4, which applies the power rule as if the inner function were x itself - the rule d/dx x^n = n x^(n-1) is a statement about x, and the chain rule is what extends it to any other base. Third, they mix the three rules up structurally: writing (uv)' = u'v' or (f(g))' = f'(g') is the same underlying error, a belief that differentiation distributes across whatever operation is in front of them. Only sums and differences behave that way, which is exactly why sums get a one-line rule and products, quotients and compositions get three separate ones. A quieter failure is not recognising a function as composite at all - sqrt(3x + 1), e^(x^2) and ln(5x) all look atomic until the outer and inner pieces are named.
whyQuestions: Why is d/dx sin(3x) equal to 3cos(3x) and not cos(3x) - where does the 3 physically come from?
Why does the power rule d/dx x^n = n x^(n-1) NOT directly give the derivative of (x^2 + 1)^5, and what has to be added?
Why does differentiation distribute across a sum but not across a product, a quotient or a composition?
Why does dy/dx = (dy/du)(du/dx) look like cancelling du, and why is that a useful mnemonic but not a proof?
Why does a three-layer problem like sin^2(3x + 1) need the rule applied twice, and how do you know when to stop?
recapCandidates.goodAnswerContains: States the rule in both notations and names the parts: d/dx[f(g(x))] = f'(g(x)) times g'(x), equivalently dy/dx = (dy/du)(du/dx) with u = g(x) - differentiate the outer function leaving the inner one untouched, then multiply by the derivative of the inner. Explains why the factor is there: if the inner function changes k times as fast as x, the composite changes k times as fast too, because the rates multiply; in sin(3x) the inner u = 3x runs three times as fast as x, so the output oscillates three times as fast. Contrasts the three rules by structure so they cannot be swapped: (uv)' = u'v + uv' (two terms added); (u/v)' = (u'v - uv')/v^2 (order matters, denominator squared); chain = outer' times inner' (multiplied); and notes that only sums and constant multiples allow term-by-term differentiation.
recapCandidates.workedExample: (1) y = (x^2 + 1)^5. Outer (.)^5, inner u = x^2 + 1: dy/du = 5u^4 and du/dx = 2x, so dy/dx = 10x(x^2 + 1)^4. Sanity check on the easy case: (x^2+1)^2 = x^4 + 2x^2 + 1 differentiates to 4x^3 + 4x = 4x(x^2+1), and the rule gives 2(x^2+1)(2x) = the same. (2) y = sqrt(3x + 1) = (3x + 1)^(1/2), so dy/dx = (1/2)(3x + 1)^(-1/2) times 3 = 3/(2 sqrt(3x + 1)); dropping the inner 3 halves the answer. (3) y = e^(x^2): outer e^u is its own derivative, inner u = x^2, so dy/dx = 2x e^(x^2) - note the answer is NOT e^(2x); the exponent is untouched and the inner derivative multiplies out front. (4) Product and chain together: y = x^3 sin(2x). Product rule with u = x^3 and v = sin(2x): u' = 3x^2 and v' needs the chain rule, giving 2cos(2x), so dy/dx = 3x^2 sin(2x) + 2x^3 cos(2x). Identify the outermost operation first - here a product - and let the pieces call whichever rule they need. (5) Chain twice: y = sin^2(3x + 1) = [sin(3x + 1)]^2. The outermost operation is a square, giving 2 sin(3x+1) times d/dx[sin(3x+1)], and that inner derivative is itself a chain, cos(3x+1) times 3. So dy/dx = 6 sin(3x + 1) cos(3x + 1). You stop when the innermost function is plain x, whose derivative is 1 - which is exactly why nobody notices the chain rule on d/dx sin x.

recapCandidates.topic: Kirchhoff's laws - the sign convention is the whole difficulty
recapCandidates.whyMisunderstood: Both laws are one sentence each and students can recite them within minutes, which produces a dangerous confidence: the laws are trivial, the bookkeeping is not, and every lost mark lives in the bookkeeping. Four things go wrong. First, students believe they must guess the current directions correctly before starting, and freeze or redraw the circuit repeatedly. The directions are assumptions; a negative answer simply means that current runs the other way and the magnitude is still right - the single most reassuring fact in the topic, and almost nobody is told it plainly. Second, the sign rule for traversing an element gets applied by feel rather than by rule: through a resistor WITH the assumed current is a drop (-IR) and against it a rise (+IR); through a battery from - to + is a rise (+emf) and from + to - a fall (-emf); and the direction you walk the loop is your choice but must stay fixed for the whole loop. Students change direction halfway, or attach the sign to the battery's orientation on the page rather than to the order in which they meet its terminals. Third, they do not count equations: a network needs one KCL equation per node minus one, plus enough KVL loops to cover every branch, so they either write too few and cannot solve, or write every possible loop and get a redundant equation that collapses to 0 = 0 and makes them think they have erred. Fourth, the physical content gets lost: KCL is charge conservation and KVL is energy conservation, and a student who knows this cannot write a loop equation with every term the same sign, because that would say energy was created going round the loop.
whyQuestions: Why is KCL a statement about conservation of charge, and what would it mean physically if it failed at a junction?
Why is it safe to ASSUME a current direction that turns out to be wrong, and what exactly does the negative sign in the answer tell you?
Why does traversing a resistor in the direction of the assumed current give -IR, while traversing a battery from - to + gives +emf regardless of which way the current flows through it?
Why does a circuit with n nodes give only n - 1 independent KCL equations, and why does the nth one add nothing?
Why does going round a loop and adding every term with the same sign guarantee you have made an error, whatever the numbers are?
recapCandidates.goodAnswerContains: States both laws with their conservation principle attached: KCL - the sum of currents entering a junction equals the sum leaving, because charge cannot accumulate at a point; KVL - the algebraic sum of potential differences round any closed loop is zero, because a charge returning to its start returns to the same potential. Gives the procedure as a fixed drill: label every branch current with an assumed direction, write KCL at all but one node, choose loops and a traversal direction and hold it, apply the sign rules (resistor -IR with the current and +IR against it; source +emf from - to + and -emf from + to -), solve the simultaneous equations, and read a negative current as right magnitude, opposite direction. Checks rather than trusts: substitute back into an unused loop, and confirm the power balance, with total power delivered by the sources equal to the total I^2 R dissipated.
recapCandidates.workedExample: (1) Two opposing emfs. A 12 V battery (r = 0.5 ohm) and a 6 V battery (r = 0.3 ohm) are in series in OPPOSITION, with an external 5.2 ohm resistor. Assume I clockwise, driven by the 12 V cell. Walking clockwise: +12 (through the 12 V cell from - to +), -I(0.5), -I(5.2), -6 (through the 6 V cell from + to -, since it opposes), -I(0.3). KVL: 12 - 6 - I(6.0) = 0, so I = 1.0 A clockwise. The 12 V cell delivers 12 W, the 6 V cell absorbs 6 W (it is being charged), and 1.0^2 times 6.0 = 6 W is dissipated: 12 = 6 + 6, which checks. (2) Two loops, and a negative answer. Two batteries feed a shared branch: emf1 = 10 V through R1 = 2 ohm into node A, emf2 = 4 V through R2 = 1 ohm into the same node A, and a common R3 = 3 ohm from A back to the shared negative rail. Assume I1 and I2 flow into A and I3 out through R3. KCL at A: I1 + I2 = I3. Left loop: 10 - 2 I1 - 3 I3 = 0. Right loop: 4 - I2 - 3 I3 = 0. Substituting I3 = I1 + I2 gives 10 = 5 I1 + 3 I2 and 4 = 3 I1 + 4 I2, so I1 = 28/11 = 2.55 A, I2 = -0.91 A and I3 = 1.64 A. The negative I2 is the point: the 4 V battery is not driving current into A at all, it is being driven backwards by the stronger branch at 0.91 A. Nothing needs redoing - the assumption was wrong and the algebra said so. Power check: sources deliver 10 times 2.55 = 25.5 W with 4 times 0.91 = 3.6 W absorbed by the reversed cell, and the dissipation 2(2.55)^2 + 1(0.91)^2 + 3(1.64)^2 is about 21.9 W, matching 25.5 - 3.6.
